title: Steamed Char Siu Bao
subtitle: Fluffy yeasted steamed buns filled with sweet barbecue pork
excerpt: These dim sum staples take patience but the result -- cloud-soft dough wrapped around sticky, sweet barbecue pork -- is worth every fold. The tangzhong method keeps the dough pillowy for days. Makes 12 buns in about 2 hours including proving time.
sourceNotes: Steamed char siu bao (barbecue pork buns) have been a fixture of Cantonese yum cha since the Song dynasty, appearing alongside har gau and siu mai as one of the essential dim sum trio. The tangzhong technique -- a cooked flour-water paste folded into yeast dough -- entered wide use in Chinese baking through Japanese influence in the 20th century and is now standard in commercial bao dough for its effect on shelf life and texture.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze steamed buns in a single layer, then transfer to a bag. Reheat from frozen in a steamer for 10 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. The tangzhong can be made the night before.

content.text: This recipe makes 12 buns and takes about 2 hours including a one-hour prove. The dough uses a
tangzhong
-- a small cooked portion of flour and water stirred into the main dough -- which keeps the buns soft and cloud-like long after they come off the steam. The filling is
char siu
pork in a sticky, sweet sauce -- shop-bought char siu works perfectly.
The most common mistake with steamed
bao dough

is under-proving. The buns should roughly double in size and feel noticeably lighter before they go into the steamer. A cold kitchen will slow the prove -- sit the tray near a warm oven if needed. Also, lift the steamer lid with a cloth so condensation drips away from the buns.
What you need
Method

Make the tangzhong first: whisk 20 g plain flour into 100 ml cold water in a small saucepan until smooth. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for about 3 minutes until the mixture thickens to a paste the consistency of mashed potato. Remove from the heat and cool to room temperature.

Make the filling. Combine the hoisin sauce, oyster sauce, light soy, sugar, and sesame oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir in the cornflour slurry (cornflour mixed with 30 ml water) and cook, stirring, until the sauce thickens -- about 2 minutes. Add the diced char siu pork, stir to coat, then remove from the heat and cool completely.

Mix the dough. Combine the flour, sugar, yeast, and baking powder in a large bowl. Add the warm milk, vegetable oil, and the cooled tangzhong. Mix to a shaggy dough, then knead for 10 minutes by hand (or 6 minutes in a stand mixer with a dough hook) until smooth and elastic. The dough should spring back when pressed.
Cover the bowl with a damp cloth and leave in a warm spot for 1 hour until the dough has roughly doubled in size.

Divide the dough into 12 equal pieces (about 40 g each). Working with one piece at a time, roll into a disc about 10 cm in diameter, thicker at the centre than the edges. Place a heaped tablespoon of filling in the centre. Gather the edges up around the filling and pleat to seal, twisting the top to close. Place sealed-side down on a square of baking paper in the steamer basket.
Leave the filled buns to prove for a further 20-30 minutes until they look puffed and feel lighter. Meanwhile, bring a large pan of water to a rolling boil.

Place the steamer basket over the boiling water. Drape a clean cloth under the lid to catch condensation, then place the lid on top. Steam for 12 minutes. Do not lift the lid during cooking. After 12 minutes, turn off the heat and leave the buns to rest in the sealed steamer for 2 minutes before serving -- this prevents the
hoisin sauce
-glazed filling from making the base soggy.

items.symptom: Buns collapsed or wrinkled after steaming
items.cause: Lid was lifted during steaming, or the buns were moved to cold air too quickly
items.fix: Always rest buns in the covered steamer for 2 minutes after turning off the heat before opening the lid.

items.symptom: Dough is dense and does not spring back
items.cause: Under-proved, or the yeast was killed by milk that was too hot
items.fix: Milk should be warm to the touch (about 38C), not hot. Prove until the dough has visibly doubled, not just expanded.

items.cause: The filling was too wet or the seal was not tight
items.fix: Cook the filling sauce until it is thick enough to mound on a spoon, not run. Pleat the dough firmly and press the top twist closed before proving.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Steamed char siu bao is a staple of Cantonese dim sum. The steamed version is softer and paler than the baked one, which has a glossy, golden crust. Bamboo steamers give the best result. A metal steamer works but condensation can drip onto the buns and wet the surface.
